Canada Goose Holdings Inc. (GOOS) is Attracting Investor Attention: Here is What You Should Know
sum: Canada Goose (GOOS) has been one of the most searched-for stocks on Zacks.com lately. So, you might want to look at some of the facts that could shape the stock's performance in the near term.

Shares of this high-end coat maker have returned +1.5% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -5.7% change. The Zacks Retail - Apparel and Shoes industry, to which Canada Goose belongs, has gained 5.4% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

Canada Goose is expected to post earnings of $1.20 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +16.5%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed -1.6%.
The consensus earnings estimate of $0.88 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +57.1%. This estimate has changed +18.9% over the last 30 days.

sum: Investor AB (publ) is a private equity firm specializing in mature, middle market, buyouts and growth capital investments. For core investments, the firm invests in health care, financial services, IT and fintech sectors, life sciences, mathematics, data, materials science, AI, quantum technology and considers investments in listed companies in leading minority positions. The firm seeks to invest globally. For its operating investments, the firm seeks to focus on medium-sized to large companies headquartered in Northern Europe. It prefers to invests in North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia-Pacific, Channel Island, Greenland, The Faroe Islands, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Jan Mayen, Svalbard, Sweden, Isle of Man, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Great Lakes, Mountain, Latin America and Caribbean region. It acquires controlling interest or minority position with significant influence in its portfolio companies within operating investments. For financial investments, it acquires minority ownership in financial holdings for shorter horizon. The firm seeks to exit its private equity investments between three years and seven years. The firm seeks to take board membership in its portfolio companies. Investor AB (publ) was founded in 1916 and is based in Stockholm, Sweden.

items.t: In Taiwan, investors 'really happy' at Jensen Huang's return
sum: Taiwanese investors rejoiced on Tuesday as the island's tech-heavy stock market soared more than nine percent following Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia less than two weeks after his abrupt exit sent shares plummeting.
Huang, who was born in Taiwan and feted like a rock star during his visits, has generated huge amounts of wealth for the island at the centre of the global AI boom.
Investors on the island have piled into the stock market this year, a growing number of them borrowing money to buy shares in the booming tech sector, as the benchmark index hit record highs.
Though many took a dim view of Huang's affair with a woman US officials suspect was working for Chinese intelligence, their greater concern was the scandal's impact on their investments.
"Seeing him come back makes me really happy," said Andy Chen, 33, who works in the education industry.
"Everyone online is joking that the 'Papa Huang incident' gave a lot of people a chance to bottom‑fish and buy in."
The Taiex plunged 17.5 percent last week, prompting the government to intervene to stabilise the market.

10.5% yield! Is this the best FTSE stock for an income-focused Stocks & Shares ISA?
sum: Building a passive income inside a Stocks and Shares ISA is one of the smartest moves an investor can make. Why? Because every penny of dividends arrives completely tax-free. And even with the stock market near record highs, there are still some juicy yields on offer right now.
Case in point: Henderson Far East Income (LSE:HFEL) currently pays just over 10%!

Please note that tax treatment depends on the individual circumstances of each client and may be subject to change in future. The content in this article is provided for information purposes only. It is not intended to be, neither does it constitute, any form of tax advice. Readers are responsible for carrying out their own due diligence and for obtaining professional advice before making any investment decisions.

Let's start with a quick introduction. Henderson Far East Income's an investment trust. It owns a diversified portfolio of quality shares across Asia, and uses the income these investments generate to fund its own payout.

This income comes from two places. The first is simply the dividends paid by the various companies it owns. The second source of cash flow is a bit more complex and stems from selling call options on the shares within its investment portfolio.

In plain English, Henderson charges other investors an upfront fee for the right to buy some of its shares at a fixed, higher price in the future. If the share price never gets there, the trust keeps both the fee and its shares. If it does, the trust has to sell at the agreed price and misses out on any gains beyond it.
In other words, it's swapping some of tomorrow's potential growth for cash in hand today. And lately, that swap's paid off handsomely.

items.t: Down 51% with a P/E of just 9.4! Why are investors suddenly buying Taylor Wimpey shares?
sum: Taylor Wimpey (LSE: TW) shares are easily the worst performing out of the 20 stocks in my Self-Invested Personal Pension (SIPP).

I had high hopes when I added them to my SIPP in November 2023. They looked cheap, with a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of around eight and a yield above 7%. The company was then in the FTSE 100, and the housing market looked ready to recover once inflation and interest rates started falling.

Then everything went wrong. The Help to Buy scheme closed in 2023, removing a source of support for first-time buyers. The Grenfell Tower disaster then left the housebuilding industry facing a huge remediation bill. Taylor Wimpey had set aside a thumping £544m for cladding and fire-safety work.

Now, the Bank of England's hiked interest rates to 4%. Higher mortgage costs, rising living expenses and uncertainty over house prices are persuading buyers to delay purchases. Buyers may be holding back in the hope that prices fall further. Build-cost inflation and labour shortages squeeze housebuilders' margins.
Taylor Wimpey shares have plunged 51% over five years and 25% in 12 months. Today, the P/E ratio is just 9.4, and the company has a market value of £2.58bn. It's now in the FTSE 250.

Given all that, I was astonished to see Taylor Wimpey's currently the third most-bought stock on the AJ Bell platform, accounting for almost 5% of all purchases. Only volatile US tech giants Anthropic and Nvidia are outselling it. Why's it suddenly in demand?

It can't be the recent trading update (11 November). Taylor Wimpey cut its 2026 UK completion forecast to 10,500 homes and warned that full-year operating profit would be at the bottom end of expectations. Its order book was down 6% to 6,839 homes.

M&S, Wetherspoons or Greggs shares: which offers the best value for UK investors?
sum: Assessing the UK's most affordable lunch might not sound like an investment strategy. But as Greggs' (LSE:GRG) shares have shown, there's big money in low-cost convenience food. Before the 2022 market downturn, the stock hit an all-time high price of £34.44 per share.
Difficult times dragged the shares to a low of £14.70 in late 2025, but they've recovered 65% since to reach £23.82. Add the 2.9% yield, and that's a decent annual return.
Impressive. But can it sustain that momentum – or could competitors like Marks & Spencer or Wetherspoon muscle in on the market?
Greggs' latest trading update in September was encouraging. Total sales rose 7.7% and like-for-like sales at company-managed shops rose 3.4%.
The differing growth metrics highlight how not only new shops are enjoying growth – existing franchising are also attracting more customers, suggesting the overall brand's gaining recognition.

But there's a bill coming. Greggs plans to spend around £60m reorganising its factories, which could save around £20m a year in running costs – but those savings will only materialise during 2028 and 2029.
Furthermore, those changes remain subject to consultation. Meanwhile, new distribution centres are set to increase costs in 2027 before supporting profitable growth.

sum: - Anthropic PBC has completed a record sized IPO, raising about $81.3b by selling 980,000,000 Class A shares at $83, valuing the AI group near $1.5t.
- The deal sits on top of an already capital intensive model. Anthropic has reported heavy net losses and sizeable long term compute commitments that tie economics directly to future Claude usage.
- We will now see how Anthropic's historic $81.3b IPO reshapes the earlier investment narrative around Claude's scale, costs and durability.
Scan how Wall Street is pricing Anthropic style AI demand by comparing ANT against 53 AI infrastructure stocks that is powering the same compute hungry trend.

Owning Anthropic PBC means believing that Claude usage can eventually outgrow the firm's heavy compute spend and large net losses. According to Michael_Jay, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the key question is whether Claude can keep acting like the "Ferrari" of enterprise AI while Anthropic leans on consumption based pricing and very high revenue retention.

The immediate catalyst is simple. Investors are watching whether post IPO demand for Claude, including newer models like Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, supports Anthropic's sizeable infrastructure commitments and funding mix. The main near term risk remains that those long term compute obligations and ongoing losses prove difficult to cover if usage plateaus or pricing pressure builds.

The most relevant recent move is Anthropic's large shelf registrations for additional Class A stock, including US$452.3b linked to ESOP related offerings. Those filings frame how management might raise further capital or bring employee equity into the tradable float, in addition to an already large IPO and existing higher risk funding profile.

items.t: Anthropic shares jump 34% in Nasdaq debut after record IPO
sum: Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) shares surged in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, opening at $111.50, up 34.3% from the artificial intelligence company's IPO price of $83, giving it a fully diluted market valuation of about $2.02 trillion.
The listing followed a record-breaking $81.34 billion public offering, which attracted demand for nearly seven times the number of shares available.
Including a separate $26 billion private placement involving seven major technology companies, Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) raised a combined $107.34 billion at its IPO price.

The private investment brought in $10 billion each from Google and Nvidia, alongside $2.5 billion from AMD and $1 billion apiece from Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) invested a further $500 million.
The private placement was separate from the public offering, with participating companies receiving non-voting shares.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei marked the listing by ringing the opening bell at Nasdaq, where he highlighted the potential of artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific and medical progress.
"I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade," Amodei said.

Tech stocks rise as Anthropic to start trading after record IPO
sum: AI titan Anthropic's shares rocketed as they started trading on Thursday but the stellar debut failed to give a wider boost to stock markets, which struggled for most of the day.

The maker of the Claude chatbot had priced its shares at $83 each, raising more than $80 billion -- topping the blockbuster initial public offering in June for Elon Musk's SpaceX -- and valuing the company at around $1.5 trillion.
But minutes after trading began on the Nasdaq in New York, the price had already topped $110 and the firm's notional value inflated to more than $2 trillion.
The stock eventually closed at $97.17, up more than 17 percent.
Analysts said that while it had been a great day for the AI giant, it was the not the same story elsewhere.
"Anthropic has had good fortune today, but the rest of the market has not," said Patrick O'Hare of Briefing.com.
"Some of it could be attributed to basically some capital redistribution and then the other element that's pressing here is the technical deterioration of the market."

GBL stock clears Recordati threshold with CVC for delisting path
sum: Groupe Bruxelles Lambert and private-equity firm CVC secured more than 90 percent of Recordati at the end of the takeover offer period, Reuters reported on November 9, 2026. The result clears the regulatory threshold for a squeeze-out of remaining minority shareholders and creates a path toward delisting the Italian pharmaceutical company from Euronext Milan.

The crossing of the threshold gives the offeror access to the compulsory purchase mechanisms under Italian takeover law. Recordati shareholders who did not tender their shares may therefore face a subsequent buyout process, while the remaining listed shares could be removed from trading after the required steps are completed.

The transaction matters for GBL because Recordati is part of its investment portfolio. Moving the holding from a listed position into a privately controlled company could change how the asset is reflected in GBL's future net asset value. The effect will depend on the final transaction terms and the valuation applied after completion.

GBL is a Brussels-based investment holding company with investments across listed and private businesses. Its portfolio includes interests in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, consumer goods and industrial activities, giving the group broader exposure than a single-industry company.

In the European investment-company segment, GBL competes for shareholder capital with diversified groups such as Eurazeo, Wendel and Investor AB. GBL is distinguished by its Belgian base and its mix of listed holdings and direct private investments.
European equity markets remain the broader backdrop for diversified investment companies. Current Euro Stoxx 50 market reports provide the relevant regional context.

sum: The Stocks and Shares ISA is one of the best tools UK investors have for building wealth almost completely tax-free, as every penny of capital gains and dividends stays in your pocket.

However, even with a powerful tool like an ISA, that still begs the question which stocks an investor should buy? After all, there are thousands of companies to choose from across stock exchanges around the world. And it can be quite daunting to try and figure out where the best place is to start.

This is where looking at what other investors are buying can be a helpful starting point. And thanks to data from Interactive Investor, we know that five of the most popular shares being bought by UK investors this year are:

Please note that tax treatment depends on the individual circumstances of each client and may be subject to change in future. The content in this article is provided for information purposes only. It is not intended to be, neither does it constitute, any form of tax advice. Readers are responsible for carrying out their own due diligence and for obtaining professional advice before making any investment decisions.

GCM Resources, Rolls-Royce and Nvidia are punchy growth stories, riding the tailwinds of booming aerospace and artificial intelligence (AI) markets. Legal & General and Glencore offer something different: higher-yielding income that pays investors for their patience.

This suggests that ISA investors are pairing potentially explosive growth opportunities with chunky passive income opportunities. And by concentrating capital into large-cap companies, investors are seemingly trying to keep risk in check. The sole outlier is GCM Resources, which is a penny stock and a different beast entirely.

As a quick introduction, GCM owns the Phulbari Coal and Power Project in north-west Bangladesh. The site holds an estimated 572 million tonnes of coal just waiting to be extracted. And just to put that number into perspective, management has estimated that it's sufficient to meet just over 60% of Bangladesh's domestic coal power demand.

Investor AB stock enters strategy execution phase after update
sum: Investor AB held its Capital Markets Update on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, putting strategy, capital allocation and the development of its portfolio companies at the center of the investor discussion. The company made the presentation materials available through its Capital Markets Update 2026 page.

Investor describes its long-term investment case through superior returns, sustainable growth, proprietary cash flow and efficient operations. The Swedish holding company links future growth at its portfolio companies to structural trends including demographics, automation, digitalization and the green transition.

The format of the update also underscores Investor's engaged-ownership model. Presentations covered listed companies, investments in EQT, Patricia Industries and several portfolio companies, including Sarnova, BraunAbility, Laborie, Nova Biomedical and Mölnlycke. That breadth keeps execution at individual holdings central to the investment debate.

On its investors and media page, Investor reported adjusted net asset value of 1,258.0 billion SEK and NAV per share of 411 SEK for the January-September 2026 period. NAV is a central reference for investors because the holding company's market quotation reflects the portfolio's underlying assets as well as expectations for future value creation.

CEO Christian Cederholm said the companies were balancing current performance with investment in innovation, particularly around artificial intelligence, to secure profitable long-term growth. For shareholders, the next test is whether those investments translate into stronger earnings and sustained NAV growth rather than only higher spending.

My Stocks and Shares ISA has tanked! Here’s what I’m doing
sum: It has been a very difficult spell for my Stocks and Shares ISA recently. Many of my largest holdings have tanked as growth and AI/tech stocks have sold off aggressively. Thursday (5 November) was particularly brutal.
Adding salt to the wounds, even 'boring' FTSE 100 stalwarts such as HSBC and BAE Systems have been struggling. Both of these are roughly 20% below their summer highs.
The first thing I need to remember is that volatility and periods of poor performance are par for the course for a long-term investor.
My holding period for a stock is three-to-five years (ideally longer). Therefore, what happens over three-to-five months isn't that important in the grand scheme of things.
That said, I'd be lying if I said I wasn't bothered when my portfolio rapidly declines in value. I don't like it. But I know it's the price of admission to the stock market.

As always, there's a Warren Buffett quote that clarifies things: "You've got to be prepared, when you buy a stock, to have it go down 50% — or more — and be comfortable with it, as long as you're comfortable with the holding."
Another thing I like to do at times like this is to put things into perspective. Returning to HSBC and BAE, for example, these UK shares had a fantastic 2025. So did Rolls-Royce.

INQ Group AB (publ) raises SEK 7 million under convertible loan facility from new US-based investment manager
sum: INQ Group AB (publ) ("INQ" or the "Company"), listed on Nasdaq Stockholm (ticker: INQ), announces that it has raised SEK 7,000,000 of additional capital under its existing secured convertible loan facility from a US-based investment manager.
The new financing is being completed on the same principal terms as the Company's most recently announced tranche of the facility, including a conversion price of SEK 0.16 per share.

The additional capital follows the conversion of substantially all of the Company's earlier convertible debt under Tranches 1 through 5. Following those conversions, approximately USD 1.55 million of convertible principal remained outstanding. The SEK 7,000,000 financing announced today will be added to that outstanding balance.
The financing further strengthens INQ's working capital position as the Company continues the commercialisation and expansion of its consumer, enterprise and education businesses.

Under the terms of the new tranche, the investor is entitled to convert outstanding principal together with accrued and unpaid interest into newly issued ordinary shares in INQ at a conversion price of SEK 0.16 per share, subject to customary adjustments.

The new tranche will also be mandatorily converted at the same conversion price upon completion of a qualified equity financing of at least USD 3 million equivalent at a subscription price of at least SEK 0.22 per share.

In connection with the new tranche, the investor will receive warrants for no further consideration with a value equal to 20 per cent of the amount funded. The warrants will entitle the holder to subscribe for new ordinary shares in INQ at a subscription price of SEK 0.32 per share for a period of two years. The final number of warrants and underlying shares will be determined in accordance with the terms of the financing.

sum: Investor AB's next major investor event is the Capital Markets Update scheduled for Wednesday, November 4, 2026, according to Vontobel Markets. The meeting gives investors a near-term opportunity to assess the holding company's portfolio priorities after its third-quarter update.

Investor's adjusted net asset value reached SEK 411 per share on September 30, 2026, up 4 percent during the third quarter and 17 percent since the start of the year. The figure exceeded the 11 percent total return delivered by the SIXRX index over the same nine-month period.

Patricia Industries was the strongest part of the portfolio in the quarter. Its private holdings generated a 15 percent total return, while adjusted EBITA increased 26 percent year over year. Aggregate sales at the private subsidiaries grew 12 percent, including 7 percent organic growth in constant currencies.

The November 4 update is expected to provide further strategic detail on Mölnlycke's planned separation into two businesses and on Patricia Industries' acquisition pipeline. The event may also help investors assess whether the recent recovery in Investor's EQT investments can continue after a difficult nine-month period.

items.t: First Solar slides 10% as Jefferies downgrades stock on lower booking visiblity
sum: Investing.com -- Shares of First Solar slumped 10% on Wed. after analysts at Jefferies said expectations for policy-driven upside in 2026 look richer than the likely reality as booking visibility weakens, and downgraded stock to Hold.
Optimism around Section 232 tariffs is likely to underwhelm investors, according to Jefferies.

The risk of carve-outs for Germany and other trading partners could dilute pricing benefits, alongside developers moving procurement decisions ahead of potential duties and foreign entity of concern rules.
These dynamics limit how much pricing uplift First Solar can realistically capture, raising downside risk to 2026 volume assumptions.
Jefferies said visibility into 2026 bookings remains limited after a difficult 2025 that saw guidance cuts, de-bookings and margin pressure.

Shares have rallied to 52-week highs, with gains of around 37% in last six months, as some regulatory headwinds eased. Jefferies sees little incremental policy support left to justify current valuations.
Investor focus is likely to shift toward execution and use of cash rather than further regulatory upside.
